title: How much work: loops inside loops
summary: Count what a script does before the data grows: one loop is n, a loop inside a loop is n × n, and a tool that reads each file once beats both.

scheme: one turn per line: n lines, n turns
text: A script that works on 10 lines can take hours on a million. To see it coming, count the work: how many times does each step run?
- A loop over a file runs once per line. n lines: n turns.
- Twice as many lines, twice the time. That's fine: the work grows like the data.
- Programmers write it O(n), read "order n".

scheme: while IFS= read -r c; do          ← n turns
while IFS= read -r m; do        ← n each
text: Put a loop inside a loop and the counts multiply: for each customer, the inner loop reads the whole newsletter again.
- n customers × n subscribers: n × n comparisons, O(n²).
- 20 times more lines on each side makes 400 times more work.
- It's the usual reason a script that was fine on a sample takes minutes or hours on the real file.
Don't guess, measure: time the script on small lists, then on lists twice as long, all of them: double only one and n × n looks like n.
- Time × 2: the work grows like n. Time × 4: like n × n, 625 times longer for 25 times the lines.
- > out.txt, not > /dev/null: GNU grep notices /dev/null and stops at the first match, so the time would lie.

scheme: the loop you see:      n turns
the loop inside grep:  up to n lines each turn
text: grep reads the newsletter each time you call it, until it finds the line: a second loop, hidden inside grep.
- At these sizes, starting a program per line (about 1 ms) costs most: 18 s for 20 000 lines. Time shows × 2, still far too slow.
- Python too: x in a_list walks the list. s = set(a_list), built once before the loop, answers x in s in one step.
Work whose answer doesn't change from one turn to the next belongs before the loop.
- Here, date gives the same day for every file: ask once, keep the answer in a variable.
- Each $( ) starts a new process, here to run date. On 50 000 files, that's 50 000 processes for one answer.

scheme: to look each line up (GNU grep)
sorted: both lists walked side by side, once
text: The fix isn't a faster loop: it's a tool that reads each file once.
- grep -Fxf: -f takes what to look for from a file, -F as plain text (a dot is just a dot), -x as whole lines.
- comm -12 shows the lines in both sorted files; <(sort file) hands them over as files (bash and zsh, not sh). Sorting costs about n × log n: 300 000 steps for 20 000 lines, not 400 million.
